**Defining extremes and trimming by minimum covering sets.** (English) [Zbl 0703.60015]

Stochastic Processes Appl. 35, No. 1, 169-180 (1990).

Given a class \(\{\ R\}\) of convex subsets of \(R^{d}\), the author defines extremes in a d-variate sample as the points of the sample that lie on the boundary of the smallest set R which contains the whole sample. Corresponding trimmed sums are then sums of all sample points omitting layers of the extremes. Representations for the distributions of these trimmed sums are obtained and used to establish necessary and sufficient conditions for consistency and asymptotic normality if the number of points removed remains bounded in probability as the sample size increases.

It turns out that, as in the one-dimensional case, this form of light trimming does not improve the asymptotic behavior of the sample mean. The general approach presented in the paper contains as special cases the minimum covering ellipse of a sample and trimming by polyhedra.

deepseek.snippet:
Martingales with barrier reflections are a fantastic way to model all kinds of parameters that are randomly distributed over time, but stay roughly the same value in the short haul. They're also very well studied, so you can make strong guarantees about their expected values and distributions, unlike naive random walks that stay within a given range.

We published a paper about such an application to modelling sensor error here: https://doi.org/10.1177/1932296817711297

The martingale comes up under the "simulator" section, starting in the paragraph "In our previous simulation study".

By "naive" random walk, I'm referring to how one would _implement_ a random walk that's restricted to a given range. The most straightforward way to do it is to "clip" any values that would exit the given range by simply coercing them to the bound, eg:

if next_value > upper_bound: next_value = upper_bound

if next_value < lower_bound: next_value = lower_bound

This works fine, but serves to concentrate probability mass near the boundaries, so it's no longer uniformly distributed. By reflecting across boundaries rather than coercing, you're effectively flattening that concentration. If you coerce, you also reduce the expected value, which may or may not be a desirable property.

## Abstract

We study Brownian motion and Brownian bridge processes conditioned to remain in a fixed interval $[0,a]$, focusing on the conditional distribution at a single time. For a Brownian motion in $[0,a]$, conditioned on survival up to time $t$ we recall (and present in a self-contained form) the conditional density of its position at $t$ (exact extrapolation). For a Brownian bridge conditioned to remain in $[0,a]$ on $[0,T]$ we express the probability density at an interior time as a normalized product of killed transition densities (exact interpolation). These densities admit dual complementary series representations, which are linked via the Jacobi theta identity. Our main contribution is a unified exact sampling suite for both extrapolation and interpolation that (i) includes boundary endpoints and (ii) automatically switches between density representations to keep acceptance rates efficient across regimes. To that end, we derive simple proposal families which cover both small- and large-time regimes, with an automatic rule selecting the tighter envelope. Our procedures extend to exact simulation of discrete skeleton paths at multiple times via the Markov property.

exa.snippet:
## Abstract

We develop an exact simulation algorithm for scalar diffusion paths and diffusion bridges when the Poisson potential is unbounded in both tails. The method reconstructs the realized range of a Brownian bridge proposal by sampling its maximum and location, together with the maxima and locations of the two adjacent restricted Brownian meanders. Conditional on this finite information, the remaining path decomposes into four conditionally independent interval-constrained Brownian bridges, which can be sampled exactly at the Poisson times required by the rejection test. In contrast to constructions based on an enclosing range layer, the proposed representation retains the exact extrema and their locations. Our algorithm returns an exact finite-dimensional skeleton without time-discretization error and permits exact post-acceptance refinement at arbitrary finite collections of times. exa-lite.title: Interval-Constrained Brownian Paths: Exact Interpolation and Extrapolation
exa-lite.snippet:
## Abstract

We study Brownian motion and Brownian bridge processes conditioned to remain in a fixed interval $[0,a]$, focusing on the conditional distribution at a single time. For a Brownian motion in $[0,a]$, conditioned on survival up to time $t$ we recall (and present in a self-contained form) the conditional density of its position at $t$ (exact extrapolation). For a Brownian bridge conditioned to remain in $[0,a]$ on $[0,T]$ we express the probability density at an interior time as a normalized product of killed transition densities (exact interpolation). These densities admit dual complementary series representations, which are linked via the Jacobi theta identity. Our main contribution is a unified exact sampling suite for both extrapolation and interpolation that (i) includes boundary endpoints and (ii) automatically switches between density representations to keep acceptance rates efficient across regimes. To that end, we derive simple proposal families which cover both small- and large-time regimes, with an automatic rule selecting the tighter envelope. Our procedures extend to exact simulation of discrete skeleton paths at multiple times via the Markov property.

exa-lite.title: Exact Simulation of Diffusions via Brownian Bridge Range Reconstruction
exa-lite.snippet:
## Abstract

We develop an exact simulation algorithm for scalar diffusion paths and diffusion bridges when the Poisson potential is unbounded in both tails. The method reconstructs the realized range of a Brownian bridge proposal by sampling its maximum and location, together with the maxima and locations of the two adjacent restricted Brownian meanders. Conditional on this finite information, the remaining path decomposes into four conditionally independent interval-constrained Brownian bridges, which can be sampled exactly at the Poisson times required by the rejection test. In contrast to constructions based on an enclosing range layer, the proposed representation retains the exact extrema and their locations. Our algorithm returns an exact finite-dimensional skeleton without time-discretization error and permits exact post-acceptance refinement at arbitrary finite collections of times. Numerical experiments validate the resulting finite-dimensional laws and identify the restricted-meander extremum simulation as the principal computational cost in the nonlinear example.

exa-lite.title: Simulation of stochastic volatility models via operator splitting schemes
exa-lite.snippet:
###### Abstract

The standard Euler discretization schemes for numerical option pricing under stochastic volatility models are known to exhibit high biases and potential unreliability. The alternative use of the exact (unbiased) simulation approach invariably involves numerical evaluation of integrated variance (and / or volatility) conditional on terminal variance (volatility) value. To resolve the technical challenge, most simulation schemes either employ the tedious Fourier inversion of conditional characteristic function or numerical approximation by moment matched distribution. We propose a general framework of constructing efficient and reliable simulation schemes for stochastic volatility models via the Strang operator splitting approximation. The simulation procedure completely circumvents the necessity of evaluation of conditional integrated variance (and / or) volatility. Our simulation schemes compete favorably well with most existing exact simulation schemes and the biased Euler schemes in terms of accuracy, efficiency, reliability and ease of implementation. Extensive numerical tests were conducted to illustrate the versatility and success of our operator splitting approach for most common stochastic volatility models, such as the Heston-type models, lifted Heston model, Hull-White model, and Barndorff-Nielsen and Shephard model. We also establish the proof of second-order convergence of the operator splitting schemes.

keenable.title: Error analysis for the numerical approximation of the quantile hedging problem
keenable.snippet:
We study the numerical approximation of the quantile hedging problem [15] in a Markovian diffusion framework modeling a complete and linear market. In this setting, the quantile hedging problem, a stochastic target problem (see [8]), writes as a stochastic control problem for an augmented state variable (X,P), where P, controlled through its volatility coefficient in a degenerate and unbounded fashion, encodes the targeted success probability and, as such, is constrained to lie in [0,1].

Quantile hedging addresses the problem of hedging a contingent claim with a prescribed probability of success. Unlike super-replication, it allows the terminal hedging error Y_T−g(X_T) to be negative on a set of positive probability, thereby reducing the required initial capital while controlling the probability of failure; see e.g. [15, 16].

keenable.title: Computer Science
keenable.snippet:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown promising results in real-world long-horizon manipulation, where memory plays a crucial role.
However, existing memory-augmented VLAs either retrieve past observations without reasoning about what they imply, or reason over the full
history in a shared context where it crowds out current perception. Cognitive science treats them as distinct systems: memory reconstructs past
experience to decide what to do, while perception guides how to act. We therefore propose ActMem, an in-context memory framework that
decouples memory reasoning from perceptual grounding within a single vision-language backbone. Built on a vision-language model with native
video understanding, ActMem infers the current subtask from a timestamped interaction history and keeps the hidden states formed during this
inference as a Latent Memory Chain-of-Thought (Memory CoT), which conditions a flow-matching action expert. Perception Attention further lets
the expert attend directly to the current view. To keep inference fast under long histories, Efficient Memory CoT Inference reuses computation
across consecutive decisions without changing the output. ActMem achieves 71.1% task success and 80.8% completion success on RoboMemArena,
surpassing the strongest baseline by 7.5 and 8.7 percentage points, and 73.8% average success on MIKASA-Robo, the best among all compared
methods. In the real world, it reaches 68.8% average success on exogenous, endogenous, and traceless memory tasks, 10.0 percentage points above
the strongest memory-augmented VLA.

keenable.title: Parareal Approximation of Stochastic 𝐿^2-Boosting
keenable.snippet:
We study Parareal approximations of stochastic L^2-boosting, reusing the learner draws of the sequential algorithm in the fine propagators. We establish mean-square error bounds whose order improves with each correction, characterize the limiting distributions of normalized errors, including non-Gaussian components and the effects of coarse discretization, and derive sufficient conditions for preserving the statistical limit laws and validation-based stopping behavior of the sequential algorithm. Numerical experiments with sample-dependent coordinate and nonlinear residual-fitting learners examine the predicted convergence rates and limiting distributions, while computational benchmarks assess the efficiency of the method relative to sequential implementations.

In mathematical finance, Bal and Maday (2002) apply Parareal to the PDE formulation of American-option pricing, while Pagès et al. (2018) combine it with least-squares Monte Carlo.

keenable.title: Operator limits of random matrices: Edge universality and sharp approximations
keenable.snippet:
Hyung-Gil Kwak∗
We establish operator universality at the spectral edge of general Wigner matrices by showing
that their suitably rescaled Lanczos tridiagonalizations, constructed from deterministic initial
vectors, converge to the stochastic Airy operator with Dirichlet boundary condition.
The result requires control of the entire tridiagonal structure on the scale relevant to the
limiting differential operator. The Lanczos coefficients for non-Gaussian Wigner matrices are
strongly dependent. We analyze their fluctuations by combining multi-resolvent local laws with
quantitative control of Krylov subspaces and a comparison of the resulting Jacobi coefficients
with those of the Gaussian ensembles. This approach identifies the limiting Brownian potential
directly from the original matrix entries, without invoking Dyson Brownian motion in the step
of Green function comparison. The resolvent limit yields joint convergence of edge eigenvalues,
embedded eigenfunctions, and spectral measures.
For Gaussian, Laguerre and circular β-ensembles we construct sharp couplings to the stochastic
Airy, Bessel and Sine operators, preserving the finite-matrix laws. For fixed β > 0, their squared
Hilbert–Schmidt inverse errors have almost-sure orders n−1/3
, n−1
and n−1
, respectively, with
a > 0 in the hard-edge upper bound. We also identify the positive leading order coefficient for
the circular ensemble, whose second derivative jumps at β = 2.

keenable.title: Variable-step-length algorithms for a random walk: hitting probability and computation performance
keenable.snippet: We present a comparative study of several algorithms for an in-plane random walk with a variable step. The goal is to check the efficiency of the algorithm in the case where the random walk terminates at some boundary. We recently found that a finite step of the random walk produces a bias in the hitting probability and this bias vanishes in the limit of an infinitesimal step. Therefore, it is important to know how a change in the step size of the random walk influences the performance of simulations. We propose an algorithm with the most effective procedure for the step-length-change protocol.

keenable.title: First-Order Sweeping Processes and Extended Projected Dynamical Systems: Equivalence, Time-Discretization and Numerical Optimal Control
keenable.snippet: Constrained dynamical systems are systems such that, by some means, the state stays within a given set. Two such systems are the (perturbed) Moreau sweeping process and the recently proposed extended Projected Dynamical System (ePDS). We show that under certain conditions solutions to the ePDS correspond to the solutions of a dynamic complementarity system, similar to the one equivalent to ordinary PDS. We then show that the perturbed sweeping process with time varying set can, under similar conditions, be reformulated as an ePDS. In this paper, we leverage these equivalences to develop an accurate discretization method for perturbed first-order Moreau sweeping processes via the finite elements with switch detection method. This allows the efficient optimal control of systems governed by ePDS and perturbed first-order sweeping processes.

keenable.title: How many states does an exact relaxation model need? Sharp state complexity and geometric obstructions for reversible chains
keenable.snippet:
How many states does a reversible Markov model need to reproduce two prescribed relaxation modes exactly? We maximize the smaller of the two stationary coordinate variances over all finite reversible chains whose states lie in a given convex region and whose coordinates relax at rates 1 and ρ. Detailed balance turns this into the equilibrium of a tension-only cable network whose loads depend on the stationary masses.
For the moment curve of the Wright–Fisher diffusion no finite chain is optimal: maximizing sequences converge to a unique beta law, and the best deficit with N states is of order N^(−2). We find the exact leading constant for states on the curve and for states in its convex hull, together with the optimal cube-root density of states. The hull constant is the curve constant times c/(1+c), c=(ρ−2)/ρ; at ρ=5/2 the hull needs √(6) times fewer states, although the limiting law is the same. For ρ>8/3 any upward enlargement of the hull lowers the constant again. All lower bounds hold for arbitrary transition graphs.

Suppose a reversible model must reproduce two prescribed modes *exactly*, and its states must stay in a prescribed region of observable space. How much stationary fluctuation can such a model carry, and how many states does it need to come close to that limit?

This paper introduces time-continuous numerical schemes to simulate sto-
chastic diﬀerential equations (SDEs) arising in mathematical ﬁnance, population
dynamics, chemical kinetics, epidemiology, biophysics, and polymeric ﬂuids. These
schemes are obtained by spatially discretizing the Kolmogorov equation associated

keenable.title: arxiv.org/pdf/1609.07206v2
keenable.snippet:
Two diﬀerent ways of trimming the sample path of a stochastic process in D[0, 1]: global
(“trim as you go”) trimming and record time (“lookback”) trimming are analysed to ﬁnd
conditions for the corresponding operators to be continuous with respect to the (strong) J1-
topology. A key condition is that there should be no ties among the largest ordered jumps

problem.

keenable.title: Multilevel Monte Carlo methods for positivity-preserving approximations of the Heston 3/2-model
keenable.snippet: This article is concerned with the multilevel Monte Carlo (MLMC) methods for approximating expectations of some functions of the solution to the Heston 3/2-model from mathematical finance, which takes values in $(0, \infty)$ and possesses superlinearly growing drift and diffusion coefficients. To discretize the SDE model, a new Milstein-type scheme is proposed to produce independent sample paths. The proposed scheme can be explicitly solved and is positivity-preserving unconditionally, i.e., for any time step-size $h>0$. This positivity-preserving property for large discretization time steps is particularly desirable in the MLMC setting. Furthermore, a mean-square convergence rate of order one is proved in the non-globally Lipschitz regime, which is not trivial, as the diffusion coefficient grows super-linearly. The obtained order-one convergence in turn promises the desired relevant variance of the multilevel estimator and justifies the optimal complexity $\mathcal{O}(ε^{-2})$ for the MLMC approach, where $ε> 0$ is the required target accuracy. Numerical experiments are finally reported to confirm the theoretical findings.

keenable-realtime.snippet: This article is concerned with the multilevel Monte Carlo (MLMC) methods for approximating expectations of some functions of the solution to the Heston 3/2-model from mathematical finance, which takes values in $(0, \infty)$ and possesses superlinearly growing drift and diffusion coefficients. To discretize the SDE model, a new Milstein-type scheme is proposed to produce independent sample paths. The proposed scheme can be explicitly solved and is positivity-preserving unconditionally, i.e., for any time step-size $h>0$. This positivity-preserving property for large discretization time steps is particularly desirable in the MLMC setting. Furthermore, a mean-square convergence rate of order one is proved in the non-globally Lipschitz regime, which is not trivial, as the diffusion coefficient grows super-linearly. The obtained order-one convergence in turn promises the desired relevant variance of the multilevel estimator and justifies the optimal complexity $\mathcal{O}(ε^{-2})$ for the MLMC approach, where $ε> 0$ is the required target accuracy. Numerical experiments are finally reported to confirm the theoretical findings.

Mathematics > Numerical Analysis

    Title:Unconditionally positivity-preserving explicit order-one strong approximations of financial SDEs with non-Lipschitz coefficients
View PDF HTML (experimental)Abstract:In this paper, we are interested in positivity-preserving approximations of stochastic differential equations (SDEs) with non-Lipschitz coefficients, arising from computational finance and possessing positive solutions. By leveraging a Lamperti transformation, we develop a novel, explicit, and unconditionally positivity-preserving numerical scheme for the considered financial SDEs. More precisely, an implicit term c_{-1}Y_{n+1}^{-1} is incorporated in the scheme to guarantee unconditional positivity preservation, and a corrective operator is introduced in the remaining explicit terms to address the challenges posed by non-Lipschitz (possibly singular) coefficients of the transformed SDEs. By finding a unique positive root of a quadratic equation, the proposed scheme can be explicitly solved and is shown to be strongly convergent with order 1, when used to numerically solve several well-known financial models such as the CIR process, the Heston-3/2 volatility model, the CEV process and the Aït-Sahalia model. Numerical experiments validate the theoretical findings.

Title: Sample Truncation for Scenario Approach to Closed-loop Chance Constrained Trajectory Optimization for Linear Systems

Authors: Hossein Sartipizadeh , Behçet Açikmeşe
View PDF
Abstract: This paper studies closed-loop chance constrained control problems with disturbance feedback (equivalently state feedback) where state and input vectors must remain in a prescribed polytopic safe region with a predefined confidence level. We propose to use a scenario approach where the uncertainty is replaced with a set of random samples (scenarios). Though a standard form of scenario approach is applicable in principle, it typically requires a large number of samples to ensure the required confidence levels. To resolve this drawback, we propose a method to reduce the computational complexity by eliminating the redundant samples and, more importantly, by truncating the less informative samples. Unlike the prior methods that start from the full sample set and remove the less informative samples at each step, we sort the samples in a descending order by first finding the most dominant ones. In this process the importance of each sample is measured via a proper mapping. Then the most dominant samples can be selected based on the allowable computational complexity and the rest of the samples are truncated offline. The truncation error is later compensated for by adjusting the safe regions via properly designed buffers, whose sizes are functions of the feedback gain and the truncation error.

# Stiffness of random walks with reflecting boundary conditions

Sascha Kaldasch [](orcid.org/0000-0002-9906-7568) and Andreas Engel

PDF

Phys. Rev. E **105** , 034132 – **Published 23 March, 2022**

DOI: doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevE.105.034132

Export Citation

Show metrics

## Abstract

We study the distribution of occupation times for a one-dimensional random walk restricted to a finite interval by reflecting boundary conditions. At short times the classical bimodal distribution due to Lévy is reproduced with walkers staying mostly either to the left or right of the initial point. With increasing time, however, the boundaries suppress large excursions from the starting point, and the distribution becomes unimodal, converging to adistribution in the long-time limit. An approximate spectral analysis of the underlying Fokker-Planck equation yields results in excellent agreement with numerical simulations.

## Can You Interpret an SDE? A Stochastic Calculus Diagnostic

If you are applying to MFE or MSFE programs, you can probably read a stochastic differential equation aloud: a drift term, a volatility term, a Brownian motion at the end. Interpreting one is a harder and more useful skill. It means looking at the equation and committing, before any code runs, to what its paths will do: where they go on average, how fast they spread out, which values they can never reach, and what they look like after a long time. That is what an interviewer is testing when they hand you an unfamiliar model and ask "what does this process do?", and it is what a first course in stochastic calculus assumes you can do by the time SDEs appear.

This post is a diagnostic you can run on yourself. It gives a six-item checklist, applies it to two SDEs you are unlikely to have memorised (a recovery rate that must stay between 0 and 1, and a commodity price that mean-reverts in logs), and then checks every prediction against 20,000 simulated paths. If your predictions match the simulation, you can interpret SDEs. If they do not, the item you missed tells you what to study next.

Drop a Brownian particle at zero and draw a line at level *a* above it. Two questions sound almost identical: *will* the particle ever touch the line, and *how long* should you expect to wait? The first has the cleanest possible answer, yes, with probability one. The second has one of the most counter-intuitive answers in probability: the expected wait is infinite. This blog is about the random time that sits between those two answers, the first-passage time, and about why its strange distribution matters for anyone who models default, barrier options or stop-loss rules.

## 1. What a First-Passage Time Is

Let Wt be a standard Brownian motion started at W0 = 0, and fix a level *a* > 0. The **first-passage time** to *a* is

*τa = inf { *t* ≥ 0 : Wt = *a* }*

with the convention that the infimum of an empty set is +∞ (the level is never reached). Because Brownian paths are continuous, the path cannot jump over the level, so “first time Wt equals *a*” and “first time Wt is at least *a*” are the same random time. That is not true for jump processes, and it is one reason first-passage results for Brownian motion are so clean.

τa is a **stopping time**: whether it has happened by time *t* can be decided by looking only at the path up to time *t*. You never need tomorrow's price to know that the barrier was touched today. ## Introduction: The Last Step in the Series

Across this series we have solved growth equations, mean-reversion equations, interest-rate equations, default-intensity equations and wealth equations — all of them ordinary differential equations, all of them producing exactly one path from any starting point. Markets do not behave like that. This closing piece is the bridge: what genuinely changes when you bolt a Brownian increment onto an ODE, why the chain rule you learned at eighteen stops working the moment you do, what replaces it and where the ODEs you already know survive untouched inside the stochastic world. It is a translation guide, not a second course in stochastic calculus.

Start with the ODE that opened the series: d*S*/d*t* = μ*S*. Rewrite it in differential form as d*S* = μ*S* d*t*. Now add one term:

## What the Monte Carlo method calculates

In financial practice, the Monte Carlo method means repeating numerical experiments with random numbers many times and finding a target value from the many results1. For pricing, it approximates the price of a derivative by the average of many results generated with random numbers. Consider a hypothetical example in which the underlying asset price is 100, the strike price is 100, expiry is 1 year away, the interest rate is 1%, and volatility is 20%. These are the conditions of the example used throughout the option valuation chapter. Valuing the call option with 10,000 paths gives an estimate of 8.33. The value given by the Black-Scholes model formula (the analytic price) is 8.43, a difference of 0.102.

Under risk-neutral valuation, the price is the discounted expected value of the payoff (the amount received) at expiry. The Monte Carlo method replaces this expected value with the average payoff over paths generated with random numbers. The paths are therefore generated with the expected return of the underlying set to the risk-free rate3. How this setting differs from the scenarios used to forecast future values is covered in Risk-Neutral Valuation.

In financial practice, the Monte Carlo method is used both to find the mean of a distribution, as with derivative prices, and to find a point in the tail of a distribution, as with value at risk (VaR). Both follow the same steps: generate changes in the underlying price with random numbers, calculate values or profits and losses from them, and aggregate the results1.

## Discrete-Time vs Continuous-Time Stochastic Processes

Every stochastic process answers two questions: what can the random quantity do, and *when* is it allowed to do it? The second question is the one people skip. A discrete-time process moves only on a fixed list of dates, such as trading days, month-ends or year-ends. A continuous-time process is defined at every instant, and its value at 10:31:07 on a Tuesday is as meaningful as its value at the close. This article is about that choice of clock: how a discrete random walk turns into Brownian motion as the steps shrink, what survives the limit and what does not, and when the discrete version is not an approximation at all but the more truthful model.

## 1. Two Clocks: What Time Means in a Stochastic Process

Formally, a stochastic process is a family of random variables *X*t indexed by time. If the index set is a countable list of dates, *t* = 0, 1, 2, and so on, the process lives in discrete time. A process can have discrete values in continuous time (a Poisson count of defaults that jumps by one at random instants) or continuous values in discrete time (a daily return drawn from a normal distribution). Most introductions describe a stochastic process as a collection of random variables, one for each moment in time: the price at 10:00, the price at 10:01, and so on. That description is correct, and it is how you first compute anything. But it hides the view that actually matters for pricing exotic derivatives, for validating a Monte Carlo engine and for understanding why continuous-time finance needs so much careful mathematics. In that second view a stochastic process is **one random object**: an entire function of time, drawn all at once. This article develops that view, explains which space of functions the draw lives in, shows that almost every interesting payoff is a *functional* of the drawn path, and then measures, on 200,000 simulated paths, how different four such functionals can be even when they are built from exactly the same randomness.

## Solving SDEs Numerically Using Euler-Maruyama Method

## Introduction

Stochastic Differential Equations (SDEs) are at the heart of modeling systems that evolve under the influence of randomness. From the unpredictable motion of stock prices in financial markets to the thermal fluctuations of particles in physical systems, SDEs provide a mathematical framework for describing dynamics that combine deterministic trends with random perturbations. While ordinary differential equations (ODEs) describe systems whose future is entirely determined by their present state, SDEs acknowledge that real-world systems are constantly buffeted by noise, uncertainty, and unpredictable external influences.

Unlike ODEs, most SDEs do not have closed-form analytical solutions. Even relatively simple-looking equations can become intractable once a stochastic term is introduced. This is where numerical methods become indispensable. Among the many numerical schemes developed for SDEs, the Euler-Maruyama method stands out as the simplest, most intuitive, and most widely used approach. It serves as the stochastic analogue of the classical Euler method for ODEs, extending the idea of small, discrete time steps to account for randomness.

In this blog, we will explore the theory behind SDEs, understand why numerical methods are necessary, derive the Euler-Maruyama scheme step by step, discuss its convergence properties, walk through a practical implementation, and examine its strengths, limitations, and alternatives. ## Approximation Error in Quantitative Finance

Every number a quantitative finance desk produces is wrong. Not wrong in the sense of careless — wrong in the sense that it is a deliberate, controlled substitute for a quantity that either cannot be computed exactly or would cost too much to compute exactly. The Greeks on a trader's screen, the VaR figure in the overnight risk report, the CVA on a twenty-year swap: each is the output of a chain of approximations, and each carries an **approximation error** that somebody, somewhere, decided was tolerable.

The professional skill is not avoiding approximation error. It is knowing its size, its sign, and how it behaves when you change the inputs. A quant who can say “this figure is accurate to about 30 basis points and the error grows linearly in maturity” is vastly more useful than one who reports eight decimal places with no idea which of them mean anything.

## 1. What Approximation Error Actually Is

Approximation error is the gap between the quantity you *wanted* and the quantity you *computed*, where the gap arises because you deliberately replaced a hard mathematical object with an easier one. If the true value is $f$ and your approximation is $\hat{f}$, the error is

$$E = \hat{f} - f$$

with absolute error $|E|$ and relative error $|E|/|f|$. The distinction between those two matters more than beginners expect, and it is worth reading the dedicated treatment in Absolute Error vs Relative Error before you design any tolerance in a production system. A 1-cent error on a USD 100 bond is immaterial; the same 1-cent error on a swap whose net present value happens to sit at USD 0.03 is catastrophic.

ultimate.title: Error analysis for the numerical approximation of the quantile hedging problem
ultimate.snippet:
We study the numerical approximation of the quantile hedging problem [15] in a Markovian diffusion framework modeling a complete and linear market. In this setting, the quantile hedging problem, a stochastic target problem (see [8]), writes as a stochastic control problem for an augmented state variable (X,P), where P, controlled through its volatility coefficient in a degenerate and unbounded fashion, encodes the targeted success probability and, as such, is constrained to lie in [0,1].

Quantile hedging addresses the problem of hedging a contingent claim with a prescribed probability of success. Unlike super-replication, it allows the terminal hedging error Y_T−g(X_T) to be negative on a set of positive probability, thereby reducing the required initial capital while controlling the probability of failure; see e.g. [15, 16].

ultimate.snippet:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown promising results in real-world long-horizon manipulation, where memory plays a crucial role.
However, existing memory-augmented VLAs either retrieve past observations without reasoning about what they imply, or reason over the full
history in a shared context where it crowds out current perception. Cognitive science treats them as distinct systems: memory reconstructs past
experience to decide what to do, while perception guides how to act. We therefore propose ActMem, an in-context memory framework that
decouples memory reasoning from perceptual grounding within a single vision-language backbone. Built on a vision-language model with native
video understanding, ActMem infers the current subtask from a timestamped interaction history and keeps the hidden states formed during this
inference as a Latent Memory Chain-of-Thought (Memory CoT), which conditions a flow-matching action expert. Perception Attention further lets
the expert attend directly to the current view. To keep inference fast under long histories, Efficient Memory CoT Inference reuses computation
across consecutive decisions without changing the output. ActMem achieves 71.1% task success and 80.8% completion success on RoboMemArena,
surpassing the strongest baseline by 7.5 and 8.7 percentage points, and 73.8% average success on MIKASA-Robo, the best among all compared
methods. In the real world, it reaches 68.8% average success on exogenous, endogenous, and traceless memory tasks, 10.0 percentage points above
the strongest memory-augmented VLA.

ultimate.title: Parareal Approximation of Stochastic 𝐿^2-Boosting
ultimate.snippet:
We study Parareal approximations of stochastic L^2-boosting, reusing the learner draws of the sequential algorithm in the fine propagators. We establish mean-square error bounds whose order improves with each correction, characterize the limiting distributions of normalized errors, including non-Gaussian components and the effects of coarse discretization, and derive sufficient conditions for preserving the statistical limit laws and validation-based stopping behavior of the sequential algorithm. Numerical experiments with sample-dependent coordinate and nonlinear residual-fitting learners examine the predicted convergence rates and limiting distributions, while computational benchmarks assess the efficiency of the method relative to sequential implementations.

In mathematical finance, Bal and Maday (2002) apply Parareal to the PDE formulation of American-option pricing, while Pagès et al. (2018) combine it with least-squares Monte Carlo.

ultimate.title: Variable-step-length algorithms for a random walk: hitting probability and computation performance
ultimate.snippet: We present a comparative study of several algorithms for an in-plane random walk with a variable step. The goal is to check the efficiency of the algorithm in the case where the random walk terminates at some boundary. We recently found that a finite step of the random walk produces a bias in the hitting probability and this bias vanishes in the limit of an infinitesimal step. Therefore, it is important to know how a change in the step size of the random walk influences the performance of simulations. We propose an algorithm with the most effective procedure for the step-length-change protocol.

ultimate.title: First-Order Sweeping Processes and Extended Projected Dynamical Systems: Equivalence, Time-Discretization and Numerical Optimal Control
ultimate.snippet: Constrained dynamical systems are systems such that, by some means, the state stays within a given set. Two such systems are the (perturbed) Moreau sweeping process and the recently proposed extended Projected Dynamical System (ePDS). We show that under certain conditions solutions to the ePDS correspond to the solutions of a dynamic complementarity system, similar to the one equivalent to ordinary PDS. We then show that the perturbed sweeping process with time varying set can, under similar conditions, be reformulated as an ePDS. In this paper, we leverage these equivalences to develop an accurate discretization method for perturbed first-order Moreau sweeping processes via the finite elements with switch detection method. This allows the efficient optimal control of systems governed by ePDS and perturbed first-order sweeping processes.

ultimate.title: How many states does an exact relaxation model need? Sharp state complexity and geometric obstructions for reversible chains
ultimate.snippet:
How many states does a reversible Markov model need to reproduce two prescribed relaxation modes exactly? We maximize the smaller of the two stationary coordinate variances over all finite reversible chains whose states lie in a given convex region and whose coordinates relax at rates 1 and ρ. Detailed balance turns this into the equilibrium of a tension-only cable network whose loads depend on the stationary masses.
For the moment curve of the Wright–Fisher diffusion no finite chain is optimal: maximizing sequences converge to a unique beta law, and the best deficit with N states is of order N^(−2). We find the exact leading constant for states on the curve and for states in its convex hull, together with the optimal cube-root density of states. The hull constant is the curve constant times c/(1+c), c=(ρ−2)/ρ; at ρ=5/2 the hull needs √(6) times fewer states, although the limiting law is the same. For ρ>8/3 any upward enlargement of the hull lowers the constant again. All lower bounds hold for arbitrary transition graphs.

Suppose a reversible model must reproduce two prescribed modes *exactly*, and its states must stay in a prescribed region of observable space. How much stationary fluctuation can such a model carry, and how many states does it need to come close to that limit?

webiq.title: Researchers develop data-guided simulations for more accurate modeling of random systems
webiq.snippet:
A classic example of randomness in dynamics is Brownian motion: the irregular movement of pollen particles suspended in water, driven by collisions with surrounding molecules. Unlike purely deterministic systems, where the trajectory is smooth and predictable, stochastic processes combine random fluctuations with an underlying trend. To study such phenomena, researchers use stochastic differential equations (SDEs).

Even though the behavior is continuous in time, we observe it only at discrete points, often corrupted by measurement noise.

"The central aim is parameter inference: estimating the parameters of these models in a Bayesian framework by computing their posterior distribution given the data. However, because the likelihood function is analytically intractable, standard statistical tools cannot be applied directly," says Jovanovski.

Approximate Bayesian computation (ABC) is a branch of Bayesian statistics that relies on generating simulated data and then assessing how close the simulations are to the observed data. In the SDE context, the idea is to simulate parameters, generate trajectories under those parameters, and retain the simulations that are sufficiently close to the observed data.

Some trajectories may be rejected simply due to randomness rather than because the parameters are poor. To address this, a data-conditional framework has been developed: instead of simulating trajectories entirely from the SDE, the simulations are conditioned directly on the observed data.

These methods have been applied, for example, to the highly variable Schlögl model, which exhibits noise-induced bistability, and in this challenging case, inference was obtained. In addition, new splitting schemes for chemical reaction networks have been introduced that preserve structural properties which standard numerical methods fail to capture. Overall, these advances reduce simulation rejection rates and enable faster, more reliable inference for stochastic dynamical systems.
